contentfulBlogPost.title: MyEquifax Registration Flow Optimisation

childMarkdownRemark.html:
Project overview

  • Team: Product Manager (Consumer Solutions), Front-end Engineering, Compliance & Information Security, Customer Care
  • Core skills demonstrated: Behavioural analytics (Glassbox), conversion rate optimisation (CRO), responsive UI design (Figma), design system scaling, accessibility compliance (WCAG 2.1)

What this project proves about me: I bridge data-driven CRO analysis and human-centred UX design in highly regulated fintech environments, translating granular user friction into measurable funnel performance gains.

The challenge

The registration funnel serves as the primary gateway to MyEquifax consumer credit services. Prospective users must supply sensitive personal and financial information to verify their identity against credit bureau databases before accessing their credit score and statutory credit report.

When I joined the initiative, the onboarding funnel exhibited steep abandonment rates, driven by several compounding operational and UX issues:

  • High cognitive load: Users were presented with extensive batches of single-line input fields on unsegmented screens without visual prioritisation or progression cues.
  • Ambiguous data requirements: Regulatory identity checks require detailed address history and personal identification, but the interface offered zero microcopy explaining why sensitive data was required, prompting severe privacy and security concerns.
  • Error recovery failure: Form validation triggered only after an explicit, full-page submit action rather than inline. When validation failed, forms often wiped entered fields, creating dead ends.
  • Accessibility debt: Critical interactive elements failed colour contrast checks and lacked semantic ARIA attributes, creating non-compliance risks under Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG 2.1 AA) and locking out assistive tech users.

Figure 1: Production view of the original mobile registration screen during device testing.

My process

I structured the onboarding overhaul across six iterative stages to align compliance, technology, and user experience objectives:

  1. Quantitative & Behavioural Discovery: Diagnosing conversion drop-off points with Glassbox session analytics and click/scroll heatmaps.
  2. Qualitative Research & Audits: Auditing user support tickets, sentiment surveys, and checking interfaces against WCAG 2.1 AA criteria.
  3. Problem Framing & Target Definition: Establishing commercial conversion benchmarks, security compliance constraints, and trust thresholds alongside Product and Legal.
  4. Information Architecture & Iterative Wireframing: Re-grouping inputs into a multi-step progressive disclosure framework, defining inline validation rules, and structuring responsive wireframes.
  5. High-Fidelity Prototyping & Design System Alignment: Translating journeys into a fully specified Figma component library with strict tokens, typography hierarchy, and state variants.
  6. Validation, Rollout & Cross-Product Scaling: Evaluating pre-launch usability, conducting accessibility QA, supporting front-end engineering handoff, and deploying the unified design pattern across adjacent consumer properties.

What I did

1. Research and bottleneck diagnosis

I audited user behaviour across the funnel using Glassbox session replays and scroll heatmaps. The behavioural data revealed acute hesitation loops: users regularly paused on address verification, struggled with birth-date formatting, and hesitated at marketing consent inputs.

Supplementing this with support ticket logs and Qualtrics survey feedback, I identified a critical psychological barrier: customers routinely questioned whether registering would trigger a "hard" credit search that would harm their credit score. The absence of reassurance microcopy directly suppressed completion rates.

Figure 2: Annotated UX audit identifying drop-off zones, layout crowding, and form interaction friction across mobile and desktop breakpoints.

2. Architectural redesign & form optimisation

Collaborating directly with the Consumer Solutions Product Manager and Front-end Engineering squads, I re-architected the form architecture from first principles:

  • Progressive disclosure: Replaced the sprawling single-page layout with a guided 3-stage model, segmenting personal details, security credentials, and identity verification.
  • Form field consolidation: Grouped interdependent fields logically, removed non-essential optional inputs, and introduced predictive address lookup to accelerate completion.
  • Dynamic validation: Implemented immediate inline validation with plain-language, real-time error recovery states, surfacing clear password criteria upfront.
  • Trust markers and microcopy: Embedded explicit reassurance microcopy confirming that registration initiates only a soft search that does not affect credit scores, positioned alongside bank-grade security indicators.

Figure 3: Detailed UI breakdown showing input grouping, reassurance microcopy, and dynamic validation states designed to streamline entry.

3. Comparing baseline against the redesign

Evaluating the baseline against the redesigned flow verified that structural simplification cleared visual noise and dramatically lowered cognitive load across both desktop and mobile screens.

Figure 4: Side-by-side comparison of the legacy registration interface against the streamlined, modernised MyEquifax layout.

4. Cross-platform expansion

To ensure consumers experienced a reliable and unified interface pattern across all Equifax digital touchpoints, I extended the modernised registration architecture, form patterns, and responsive components into adjacent portfolio tools, including WebDefend and the Statutory Credit Report access journey.

Figure 5: Rollout of the unified registration pattern to adjacent products, establishing cohesive form behaviour across the consumer ecosystem.

5. Stakeholder communication and operational handoff

Balancing financial compliance, information security, and engineering feasibility required rigorous specifications. I built comprehensive interactive Figma prototypes mapping out every dynamic state: default, focus, hover, disabled, success, and contextual error handling.

Figure 6: Component specification board mapping form states, copy variants, and accessibility requirements for development handoff.

Why I made these decisions

Figure 7: The redesigned responsive onboarding flow on desktop and mobile viewports, featuring explicit step-by-step guidance and clear field hierarchy.

  1. Swapping post-submission errors for inline guidance: In session recordings, post-submit page reloads consistently caused users to abandon the funnel, especially when password rules were not surfaced beforehand. Inline validation eliminated this guesswork.
  2. Introducing credit-score reassurance messaging: User feedback revealed fear that the registration search would reduce credit scores. Clarifying in microcopy that this constitutes an unrecorded "soft search" addressed the single biggest psychological blocker to completion.
  3. Deconstructing into a stepped model: Funnel benchmarking showed that monolithic forms overwhelmed users on mobile devices. Chunking into 3 focused stages lowered the perceived cost of beginning the flow.
  4. WCAG 2.1 compliance as a non-negotiable standard: Accessible colour contrasts, clear focus outlines, and programmatic label associations ensured the product complied with legal requirements while reducing errors for keyboard and assistive tech users.

Impact / results

Area Baseline State Post-Optimisation Result
Registration conversions High drop-off during initial data input Measurable increase in completed account registrations
Form abandonment Concentrated drop-outs at identity entry Noticeable reduction in field-level hesitation and abandonment
Accessibility Fragmented field labels and poor contrast Full WCAG 2.1 AA compliance across all onboarding viewports
User satisfaction Recurring support tickets around error loops Substantial improvement in post-launch qualitative satisfaction
Ecosystem scalability Disparate legacy patterns across consumer properties Reusable, scalable form system adopted across tools like WebDefend

Tools and skills applied

Category Tools / skills
Research & Analytics Glassbox (session replay, heatmaps), Qualtrics, Competitor benchmarking, Quantitative funnel analysis
UI / UX Design Figma, Wireframing, Responsive Design, Design Systems, Design Tokens
CRO & Strategy Conversion Rate Optimisation (CRO), Funnel Architecture, Usability Heuristics
Accessibility & Standards WCAG 2.1 AA compliance, Form accessibility (ARIA, semantic HTML)
Collaboration & Delivery Jira, Cross-functional alignment with Product Management & Engineering

Roles performed on this project

  • UX Designer: Executed behavioural audits, journey mapping, wireframing, WCAG audits, and responsive Figma prototypes.
  • CRO Specialist: Analysed funnel drop-offs using Glassbox, identified friction drivers, and formulated testable optimisation hypotheses.
  • Web Manager: Aligned the consumer digital journey with broader digital operations, maintaining design system consistency and facilitating cross-product rollouts across the MyEquifax platform.

childMarkdownRemark.html: As Web Manager, UX Designer, and Conversion Rate Optimisation (CRO) Specialist across the MyEquifax consumer portfolio from January 2023 to March 2025, I led the comprehensive redesign and performance optimisation of the primary digital onboarding funnel. The original sign-up process suffered from elevated drop-off rates driven by redundant form fields, opaque identity validation steps, and accessibility shortfalls. Combining behavioural analytics from Glassbox, competitive benchmarking, and WCAG 2.1 compliance audits, I architected a multi-step responsive onboarding journey featuring consolidated inputs, clear feedback states, and trust-building security messaging. I partnered with Product Management and Engineering to ship and test these enhancements, reducing abandonment and scaling the design language across legacy consumer products.
